prose: The Daily Californian reports on UC Berkeley's math community reckoning with OpenAI's quasi-Riemann proof. It opens with Noam Brown's cost curve: o3's 87.5% on ARC-AGI 1 cost roughly $500,000, Astra beats it for about $20, and a problem that took OpenAI and DeepMind enormous compute for IMO gold in 2025 is now solvable by anyone with a $20/month subscription - Brown's point being that massively scaled test-time compute is a glimpse of the near future. At Berkeley, mathematicians including Fields medalist Richard Borcherds are weighing what this means for the field; Borcherds admits he did not expect capabilities of this caliber so soon. The department stands at a crossroads between embracing AI tools and defending what human mathematics is for.
highlights: Berkeley's math community weighs AI after the quasi-Riemann proof
Noam Brown: o3's ARC-AGI score cost ~$500K; Astra beats it for ~$20
Brown: 2025's IMO gold took enormous compute; 2026's is a $20/month subscription
Fields medalist Richard Borcherds didn't expect this caliber so soon
The department debates embracing AI vs. redefining what human math is for
